Jeffrey Preston Bezos (/ˈbeɪzoʊs/ BAY-zohss;[2] né Jorgensen; born January 12, 1964) is an American businessman, and the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon, the world's largest e-commerce and cloud computing company. According to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index and Forbes, he was the world's wealthiest person from 2017 to 2021,[3] and in 2026, his net worth was approximately US$284 billion.[4] He is commonly considered part of the global elite.[5][6][7]
Bezos was born in Albuquerque, and raised in Houston and Miami. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with a degree in engineering. He worked on Wall Street in a variety of related fields from 1986 to early 1994. He founded Amazon in mid-1994 on a road trip from New York City to Seattle. The company began as an online bookstore and expanded to a variety of other e-commerce products and services, including video and audio streaming, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence. It is the world's largest online sales company, the largest Internet company by revenue, and the largest provider of virtual assistants and cloud infrastructure services through its Amazon Web Services branch.
Bezos founded the aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company Blue Origin in 2000, and he flew into space on Blue Origin NS-16 in 2021. He purchased the major American newspaper The Washington Post in 2013 and manages many other investments through his venture capital firm, Bezos Expeditions.
The first centibillionaire on the Forbes Real Time Billionaires Index, Bezos was named the "richest man in modern history" after his net worth increased to $150 billion in July 2018 (equivalent to $1.9×1011 in 2025).[8] On July 5, 2021, Bezos took over the role of executive chairman and stepped down as the CEO and president of Amazon, succeeded by Amazon Web Services CEO Andy Jassy.
Early life and education

Bezos was born Jeffrey Preston Jorgensen on January 12, 1964, in Albuquerque, New Mexico,[9] to Jacklyn (née Gise; 1946–2025) and Ted Jorgensen[10] (1944–2015). At the time of his birth, his mother was a 17-year-old high-school student and his father was 19.[11] Ted was a Danish American unicyclist[12] born in Chicago to a family of Baptists.[13] After completing high school despite challenging conditions, Jacklyn attended night school, bringing her baby with her.[14] Jeff attended a Montessori school in Albuquerque when he was two.[15]
Ted struggled with alcohol and with his finances.[16] Jacklyn left her husband to live with her parents, filing for divorce in June 1965 when Jeff was 17 months old.[17] After his parents divorced, his mother married Cuban immigrant Miguel "Mike" Bezos in April 1968.[18] Shortly after the wedding, Mike adopted 4-year-old Jeff, whose surname was then legally changed from Jorgensen to Bezos.[19] Jacklyn, her husband, and her son left the area and asked Ted to discontinue contact, to which he agreed.[20]
After Mike received his degree from the University of New Mexico, the family moved to Houston, Texas, so that he could begin working as an engineer for Exxon.[21] Jeff attended River Oaks Elementary School in Houston from fourth to sixth grade.[22] Jeff's maternal grandfather was Lawrence Preston Gise, a regional director of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) in Albuquerque.[23]

Gise retired early to his family's ranch near Cotulla, Texas, where his grandson would spend many summers in his youth[24] and which he would later purchase and expand from 25,000 acres (10,117 ha) to 160,000 acres (64,750 ha).[25][26] Jeff displayed scientific interests and technological proficiency and once rigged an electric alarm to keep his younger half-siblings out of his room.[27] The family moved to Miami, Florida, where Jeff attended Miami Palmetto High School.[28][29] In high school, he worked at McDonald's as a short-order line cook during the breakfast shift.[30]
Bezos attended the Student Science Training Program at the University of Florida. He was high school valedictorian, a National Merit Scholar,[31][32] and a Silver Knight Award winner in 1982.[31] In his graduation speech, Bezos spoke about the possibility of human space colonization. A local newspaper quoted him as saying that he hoped humanity would eventually move heavy industry and large populations into space while preserving Earth as "a huge national park".[33]
Bezos in the Princeton University yearbook, 1986
After graduating from high school in 1982, Bezos attended Princeton University. He initially majored in physics but later switched to electrical engineering and computer science.[34] In 2018, during a talk at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., Bezos revealed that, some thirty years ago, his Princeton classmate Yasantha Rajakarunanayake had defeated him in solving a mathematical problem, causing him to give up on his dreams of becoming a theoretical physicist.[35][36][37][38][39]
Bezos was a member of the Quadrangle Club, one of Princeton's 11 eating clubs.[40] Additionally, he was the president of the Princeton chapter of the Students for the Exploration and Development of Space (SEDS).[41][42] He had a 4.2 GPA[34] and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and Tau Beta Pi. Bezos graduated from Princeton in 1986 with a Bachelor of Science in Engineering (BSE), summa cum laude.[43]

Jeffrey Preston Bezos (/ˈbeɪzoʊs/ BAY-zohss;[2] né Jorgensen; born January 12, 1964) is an American businessman, and the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon, the world's largest e-commerce and cloud computing company. According to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index and Forbes, he was the world's wealthiest person from 2017 to 2021,[3] and in 2026, his net worth was approximately US$284 billion.[4] He is commonly considered part of the global elite.[5][6][7]
Bezos was born in Albuquerque, and raised in Houston and Miami. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with a degree in engineering. He worked on Wall Street in a variety of related fields from 1986 to early 1994. He founded Amazon in mid-1994 on a road trip from New York City to Seattle. The company began as an online bookstore and expanded to a variety of other e-commerce products and services, including video and audio streaming, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence. It is the world's largest online sales company, the largest Internet company by revenue, and the largest provider of virtual assistants and cloud infrastructure services through its Amazon Web Services branch.
Bezos founded the aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company Blue Origin in 2000, and he flew into space on Blue Origin NS-16 in 2021. He purchased the major American newspaper The Washington Post in 2013 and manages many other investments through his venture capital firm, Bezos Expeditions.
The first centibillionaire on the Forbes Real Time Billionaires Index, Bezos was named the "richest man in modern history" after his net worth increased to $150 billion in July 2018 (equivalent to $1.9×1011 in 2025).[8] On July 5, 2021, Bezos took over the role of executive chairman and stepped down as the CEO and president of Amazon, succeeded by Amazon Web Services CEO Andy Jassy.

texts.2:
Bezos was born Jeffrey Preston Jorgensen on January 12, 1964, in Albuquerque, New Mexico,[9] to Jacklyn (née Gise; 1946–2025) and Ted Jorgensen[10] (1944–2015). At the time of his birth, his mother was a 17-year-old high-school student and his father was 19.[11] Ted was a Danish American unicyclist[12] born in Chicago to a family of Baptists.[13] After completing high school despite challenging conditions, Jacklyn attended night school, bringing her baby with her.[14] Jeff attended a Montessori school in Albuquerque when he was two.[15]
Ted struggled with alcohol and with his finances.[16] Jacklyn left her husband to live with her parents, filing for divorce in June 1965 when Jeff was 17 months old.[17] After his parents divorced, his mother married Cuban immigrant Miguel "Mike" Bezos in April 1968.[18] Shortly after the wedding, Mike adopted 4-year-old Jeff, whose surname was then legally changed from Jorgensen to Bezos.[19] Jacklyn, her husband, and her son left the area and asked Ted to discontinue contact, to which he agreed.[20]
After Mike received his degree from the University of New Mexico, the family moved to Houston, Texas, so that he could begin working as an engineer for Exxon.[21] Jeff attended River Oaks Elementary School in Houston from fourth to sixth grade.[22] Jeff's maternal grandfather was Lawrence Preston Gise, a regional director of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) in Albuquerque.[23]
texts.3:
Gise retired early to his family's ranch near Cotulla, Texas, where his grandson would spend many summers in his youth[24] and which he would later purchase and expand from 25,000 acres (10,117 ha) to 160,000 acres (64,750 ha).[25][26] Jeff displayed scientific interests and technological proficiency and once rigged an electric alarm to keep his younger half-siblings out of his room.[27] The family moved to Miami, Florida, where Jeff attended Miami Palmetto High School.[28][29] In high school, he worked at McDonald's as a short-order line cook during the breakfast shift.[30]
Bezos attended the Student Science Training Program at the University of Florida. He was high school valedictorian, a National Merit Scholar,[31][32] and a Silver Knight Award winner in 1982.[31] In his graduation speech, Bezos spoke about the possibility of human space colonization. A local newspaper quoted him as saying that he hoped humanity would eventually move heavy industry and large populations into space while preserving Earth as "a huge national park".[33]
Bezos in the Princeton University yearbook, 1986
After graduating from high school in 1982, Bezos attended Princeton University. He initially majored in physics but later switched to electrical engineering and computer science.[34] In 2018, during a talk at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., Bezos revealed that, some thirty years ago, his Princeton classmate Yasantha Rajakarunanayake had defeated him in solving a mathematical problem, causing him to give up on his dreams of becoming a theoretical physicist.[35][36][37][38][39]
Bezos was a member of the Quadrangle Club, one of Princeton's 11 eating clubs.[40] Additionally, he was the president of the Princeton chapter of the Students for the Exploration and Development of Space (SEDS).[41][42] He had a 4.2 GPA[34] and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and Tau Beta Pi. Bezos graduated from Princeton in 1986 with a Bachelor of Science in Engineering (BSE), summa cum laude.[43]

**Peter Albert David Singer** (born 6 July 1946)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Duignan-2023-2) is an Australian moral philosopher who is Emeritus Ira W. DeCamp Professor of Bioethics at Princeton University. Singer's work specialises in applied ethics, approaching the subject from a secular, utilitarian perspective. His book _Animal Liberation_ (1975) criticized intensive animal farming and speciesism, and shaped the animal rights movement. His essay "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" argues for the moral imperative of donating to help the global poor, using the drowning child analogy. For most of his career he was a preference utilitarian. He revealed in _The Point of View of the Universe_ (2014), co-authored with Katarzyna de Lazari-Radek, that he had become a hedonistic utilitarian. His books _The Life You Can Save_ (2009) and _The Most Good You Can Do_ (2015) are influential in the effective altruism movement.
On two occasions, Singer served as chair of the philosophy department at Monash University, where he founded its Centre for Human Bioethics. In 1996, he stood unsuccessfully as a Greens candidate for the Australian Senate. In 2004, Singer was recognised as the Australian Humanist of the Year by the Council of Australian Humanist Societies. In 2005 _The Sydney Morning Herald_ placed him among Australia's ten most influential public intellectuals.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-3) Singer is a co-founder of Animals Australia and the founder of the non-profit organisation The Life You Can Save.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-4)

## Early life and education
[edit]
Singer in 2009
Peter Albert David Singer was born in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer_About-5) on 6 July 1946.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Duignan-2023-2) His parents were Austrian Jews who immigrated to Australia from Vienna after Austria's annexation (_Anschluss_) by Nazi Germany in 1938,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Thompson-2007-6) and settled in Melbourne.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer_About-5) His paternal grandparents were taken by the Nazis to Łódź, and were most likely murdered, since they were never heard from again. His maternal grandfather, the educator and psychologist David Ernst Oppenheim (1881–1943), was murdered in the Theresienstadt concentration camp.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-7) Oppenheim was a member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society and wrote a joint article with Sigmund Freud, before joining the Adlerian Society for Individual Psychology.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-8) Singer later wrote a biography of Oppenheim.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-9)

## Early life and education
Singer is an atheist and was raised in a prosperous, non-religious family.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-10) His father had a successful business importing tea and coffee.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Thompson-2007-6) His family rarely observed Jewish holidays, and Singer declined to have a bar mitzvah.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-11) Singer attended Preshil,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-12) and later Scotch College. After leaving school, Singer studied law, history, and philosophy as a resident of Ormond College at the University of Melbourne, earning a bachelor's degree in 1967.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-13) Singer explained that he elected to major in philosophy after his interest was piqued by discussions with his sister's then-boyfriend.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-14) He earned a master's degree for a thesis entitled _Why Should I Be Moral?_ at the same university in 1969. He was awarded a scholarship to study at the University of Oxford and obtained from there a Bachelor of Philosophy in 1971 with a thesis on civil disobedience supervised by R. M. Hare and published as a book in 1973.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-15) Singer names Hare, Australian philosopher H. J. McCloskey and British philosopher J. L. H. Thomas, who taught him "how to read and understand Hegel",[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-16) as his most important mentors.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-17)

A lecture at the Zoological Institute of the University of Zurich was interrupted by two groups of protesters. The first group was a group of disabled people who staged a brief protest at the beginning of the lecture. They objected to inviting an advocate of euthanasia to speak. At the end of this protest, when Singer tried to address their concerns, a second group of protesters rose and began chanting _Singer raus! Singer raus!_ ("Singer out!" in German) When Singer attempted to respond, a protester jumped on stage and grabbed his glasses, and the host ended the lecture. Singer explains "my views are not threatening to anyone, even minimally", and says that some groups play on the anxieties of those who hear only keywords that are understandably worrying (given the constant fears of ever repeating the Holocaust) if taken with any less than the full context of his belief system.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer-1993-31):346–359[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-104)
In 1991, Singer was due to speak along with R. M. Hare and Georg Meggle[de] at the 15th International Wittgenstein Symposium in Kirchberg am Wechsel, Austria. Singer has stated that threats were made to Adolf Hübner, then the president of the Austrian Ludwig Wittgenstein Society, that the conference would be disrupted if Singer and Meggle were given a platform. Hübner proposed to the board of the society that Singer's invitation, as well as the invitations of a number of other speakers, be withdrawn. In an article originally published in _The New York Review of Books_, Singer argued that the protests dramatically increased the amount of coverage he received, saying that "instead of a few hundred people hearing views at lectures in Marburg and Dortmund, several millions read about them or listened to them on television". Despite this, Singer argues that it has led to a difficult intellectual climate, with professors in Germany unable to teach courses on applied ethics and campaigns demanding the resignation of professors who invited Singer to speak.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer-2001-101)

Factary has been providing high quality research and fundraising consultancy services to not-for-profit organisations across the UK, Europe and beyond for over twenty five years.
When we were founded in 1990, we knew that fundraisers needed specialist help to uncover prospective new donors and to learn more about their existing major donors and supporters, and to understand the philanthropic landscape in which they were operating. With a background in both fundraising and research, we knew that we could help.
Since then, **Factary** has evolved into a full-service knowledge, research and information consultancy for the non-profit sector.
*   ### 1990s  
*   ### 2000s  
*   ### 2010s

## 1990s
*   Factary was founded by our current Chair, Chris Carnie, in **1990**.  
*   In **1992** we started database screening and analysis. Our initial screening process matched high-net-worth individuals using name and surname. At its height our database included over 170,000 records.  
*   In **1993** we launched **New Trust Update**, our monthly publication on newly registering grant-making trusts and foundations in the UK.  
*   In **1998** we opened our first international office in Barcelona, Spain.

## 2000s
*   In **2001** we carried out the first study into major gift fundraising in continental Europe, in Austria.  
*   In **2002** we carried out our first feasibility study in Latin America.  
*   In **2003** Chapel and York published Chris Carnie’s book _Fundraising from Europe_.  
*   In summer **2003** we carried out the first ever data screening in continental Europe screening 7,924 records for a French environmental organisation.  
*   In **2004** we were joined by Helen E Brown, our US Director and partner, and President of the Helen Brown Group.  
*   In **2004** we carried out the first ever data screening in Spain.  
*   In **December 2004** we announced our link-up with **THINK Consulting Solutions**, the leading fundraising consultancy.  
*   In **2005** we developed new directions for the company, with a new focus on:  
    *   consulting and research for philanthropists;  
    *   international consulting and research;  
    *   knowledge management; and  
    *   services to non-profits and their advisers.

*   In **2005** we were part of a consortium that carried out the first study into legacy giving in Spain.  
*   In **2006** we opened our office in Belgium. Our EU and international research is managed from this office. In this year we also screened data in Belgium for the first time.  
*   In **2006** we conducted the first study into major gift fundraising in the Netherlands.  
*   In **2006** we renewed our logo and strapline.  
*   In **February 2007** we separated from **THINK Consulting Solutions** and returned to full independence.  
*   In **2010** we launched Factary Phi, an online searchable database of donations to the UK non-profit sector, covering gifts made by individuals, trusts and foundations, and corporates. Phi is the first database of its kind designed for the UK’s non-profit sector.

## 2010s
*   In **February 2011** we published _The Venture Philanthropists_ the first study into venture philanthropy in the UK.  
*   In **April 2012** we published _Soliciting Gifts_, the first study into the Community Responsibility policies and philanthropy of the UK’s top 20 law firms.  
*   In **December 2012** we also published the first _Foundations of Wealth_, profiling 32 of the UK’s newest grant-making philanthropists, with a combined wealth of £18.2 billion. Further reports would be produced every year for the next three years.  
*   In **2014**, after consulting with subscribers, we updated the Phi database with an entirely new interface, making it streamlined and easier to search.  
*   In **2015** we published _Trust Women_, a report into the number of women on the boards of UK grant-making trusts.  
*   In **2016** we launched our New Trust Update archive, an online searchable database of all past issues of the New Trust Update, our monthly summary of newly registered UK grant-makers. The archive grants all subscribers access to all back-issues, and to special reports produced by Factary.  
*   In **2017** we published an in-depth report into the philanthropic activities of the Chairpersons of the UK’s FTSE100. 94 Chairs were profiled, along with their company, including CSR activities.  
*   In **2017** Factary’s Chair and founder, Chris Carnie, published _How Philanthropy is Changing in Europe_ (Policy Press).  
*   In **2017**, in response to regulatory changes and in order to take advantage of new technologies, we designed and pioneered a completely new way to screen and analyse supporter databases to identify major and influential donors, once again proving we are at the forefront of prospect research in the UK.

In 2005 _The Sydney Morning Herald_ placed him among Australia's ten most influential public intellectuals.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-3) Singer is a co-founder of Animals Australia and the founder of the non-profit organisation The Life You Can Save.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-4)

## Early life and education
[edit]
Singer in 2009
Peter Albert David Singer was born in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer_About-5) on 6 July 1946.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Duignan-2023-2) His parents were Austrian Jews who immigrated to Australia from Vienna after Austria's annexation (_Anschluss_) by Nazi Germany in 1938,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Thompson-2007-6) and settled in Melbourne.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer_About-5) His paternal grandparents were taken by the Nazis to Łódź, and were most likely murdered, since they were never heard from again. His maternal grandfather, the educator and psychologist David Ernst Oppenheim (1881–1943), was murdered in the Theresienstadt concentration camp.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-7) Oppenheim was a member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society and wrote a joint article with Sigmund Freud, before joining the Adlerian Society for Individual Psychology.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-8) Singer later wrote a biography of Oppenheim.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-9)
texts.3:
## Early life and education
Singer is an atheist and was raised in a prosperous, non-religious family.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-10) His father had a successful business importing tea and coffee.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Thompson-2007-6) His family rarely observed Jewish holidays, and Singer declined to have a bar mitzvah.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-11) Singer attended Preshil,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-12) and later Scotch College. After leaving school, Singer studied law, history, and philosophy as a resident of Ormond College at the University of Melbourne, earning a bachelor's degree in 1967.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-13) Singer explained that he elected to major in philosophy after his interest was piqued by discussions with his sister's then-boyfriend.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-14) He earned a master's degree for a thesis entitled _Why Should I Be Moral?_ at the same university in 1969. He was awarded a scholarship to study at the University of Oxford and obtained from there a Bachelor of Philosophy in 1971 with a thesis on civil disobedience supervised by R. M. Hare and published as a book in 1973.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-15) Singer names Hare, Australian philosopher H. J. McCloskey and British philosopher J. L. H. Thomas, who taught him "how to read and understand Hegel",[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-16) as his most important mentors.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-17)

## Early life and education
### Animal liberation and speciesism
#### Medical intervention in the aging process
A lecture at the Zoological Institute of the University of Zurich was interrupted by two groups of protesters. The first group was a group of disabled people who staged a brief protest at the beginning of the lecture. They objected to inviting an advocate of euthanasia to speak. At the end of this protest, when Singer tried to address their concerns, a second group of protesters rose and began chanting _Singer raus! Singer raus!_ ("Singer out!" in German) When Singer attempted to respond, a protester jumped on stage and grabbed his glasses, and the host ended the lecture. Singer explains "my views are not threatening to anyone, even minimally", and says that some groups play on the anxieties of those who hear only keywords that are understandably worrying (given the constant fears of ever repeating the Holocaust) if taken with any less than the full context of his belief system.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer-1993-31):346–359[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-104)
In 1991, Singer was due to speak along with R. M. Hare and Georg Meggle[de] at the 15th International Wittgenstein Symposium in Kirchberg am Wechsel, Austria. Singer has stated that threats were made to Adolf Hübner, then the president of the Austrian Ludwig Wittgenstein Society, that the conference would be disrupted if Singer and Meggle were given a platform. Hübner proposed to the board of the society that Singer's invitation, as well as the invitations of a number of other speakers, be withdrawn. The Society decided to cancel the symposium.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer-2001-101)

## Early life and education
### Animal liberation and speciesism
#### Medical intervention in the aging process
In an article originally published in _The New York Review of Books_, Singer argued that the protests dramatically increased the amount of coverage he received, saying that "instead of a few hundred people hearing views at lectures in Marburg and Dortmund, several millions read about them or listened to them on television". Despite this, Singer argues that it has led to a difficult intellectual climate, with professors in Germany unable to teach courses on applied ethics and campaigns demanding the resignation of professors who invited Singer to speak.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Singer-2001-101)
Singer was elected a corresponding fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities in 1981.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-105) He was inducted into the United States Animal Rights Hall of Fame in 2000.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-106) In June 2012, Singer was appointed a Companion of the Order of Australia (AC) for "eminent service to philosophy and bioethics as a leader of public debate and communicator of ideas in the areas of global poverty, animal welfare and the human condition".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-107) Singer received _Philosophy Now_'s 2016 Award for Contributions in the Fight Against Stupidity for his efforts "to disturb the comfortable complacency with which many of us habitually ignore the desperate needs of others ... particularly for this work as it relates to the Effective Altruism movement".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-108)

## Early life and education
### Animal liberation and speciesism
#### Medical intervention in the aging process
In 2018, Singer was cited in the book _Rescuing Ladybugs_ by author and animal advocate Jennifer Skiff as a "hero among heroes in the world" who, in arguing against speciesism "gave the modern world permission to believe what we innately know – that animals are sentient and that we have a moral obligation not to exploit or mistreat them."[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Skiff-2018-109):132 The book states that Singer's "moral philosophy on animal equality was sparked when he asked a fellow student at Oxford University a simple question about his eating habits."[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-Skiff-2018-109)
In 2021, Singer was awarded the US$1-million Berggruen Prize,[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-110) and decided to give it away. He decided in particular to give half of the prize money to his foundation The Life You Can Save, because "over the last three years, each dollar spent by it generated an average of $17 in donations for its recommended nonprofits". He added he has never taken money for personal use from the organisation. Moreover, he plans to donate more than a third of the money to organisations combating intensive animal farming, and recommended as effective by Animal Charity Evaluators.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-111)
For 2022, Singer received the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award in the category of "Humanities and Social Sciences".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-112)
Singer serves on the Executive Advisory Board of the World.Minds Foundation, contributing to global ethical discussions on science, society, and responsibility.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer#cite_note-113)

Factary has been providing high quality research and fundraising consultancy services to not-for-profit organisations across the UK, Europe and beyond for over twenty five years.
When we were founded in 1990, we knew that fundraisers needed specialist help to uncover prospective new donors and to learn more about their existing major donors and supporters, and to understand the philanthropic landscape in which they were operating. With a background in both fundraising and research, we knew that we could help.
Since then, **Factary** has evolved into a full-service knowledge, research and information consultancy for the non-profit sector.
*   ### 1990s  
*   ### 2000s  
*   ### 2010s
texts.1:
## 1990s
*   Factary was founded by our current Chair, Chris Carnie, in **1990**.  
*   In **1992** we started database screening and analysis. Our initial screening process matched high-net-worth individuals using name and surname. At its height our database included over 170,000 records.  
*   In **1993** we launched **New Trust Update**, our monthly publication on newly registering grant-making trusts and foundations in the UK.  
*   In **1998** we opened our first international office in Barcelona, Spain.
texts.2:
## 2000s
*   In **2001** we carried out the first study into major gift fundraising in continental Europe, in Austria.  
*   In **2002** we carried out our first feasibility study in Latin America.  
*   In **2003** Chapel and York published Chris Carnie’s book _Fundraising from Europe_.  
*   In summer **2003** we carried out the first ever data screening in continental Europe screening 7,924 records for a French environmental organisation.  
*   In **2004** we were joined by Helen E Brown, our US Director and partner, and President of the Helen Brown Group.  
*   In **2004** we carried out the first ever data screening in Spain.  
*   In **December 2004** we announced our link-up with **THINK Consulting Solutions**, the leading fundraising consultancy.  
*   In **2005** we developed new directions for the company, with a new focus on:  
    *   consulting and research for philanthropists;  
    *   international consulting and research;  
    *   knowledge management; and  
    *   services to non-profits and their advisers.

*   In **2005** we were part of a consortium that carried out the first study into legacy giving in Spain.  
*   In **2006** we opened our office in Belgium. Our EU and international research is managed from this office. In this year we also screened data in Belgium for the first time.  
*   In **2006** we conducted the first study into major gift fundraising in the Netherlands.  
*   In **2006** we renewed our logo and strapline.  
*   In **February 2007** we separated from **THINK Consulting Solutions** and returned to full independence.  
*   In **2010** we launched Factary Phi, an online searchable database of donations to the UK non-profit sector, covering gifts made by individuals, trusts and foundations, and corporates. Phi is the first database of its kind designed for the UK’s non-profit sector.
texts.3:
## 2010s
*   In **February 2011** we published _The Venture Philanthropists_ the first study into venture philanthropy in the UK.  
*   In **April 2012** we published _Soliciting Gifts_, the first study into the Community Responsibility policies and philanthropy of the UK’s top 20 law firms.  
*   In **December 2012** we also published the first _Foundations of Wealth_, profiling 32 of the UK’s newest grant-making philanthropists, with a combined wealth of £18.2 billion. Further reports would be produced every year for the next three years.  
*   In **2014**, after consulting with subscribers, we updated the Phi database with an entirely new interface, making it streamlined and easier to search.  
*   In **2015** we published _Trust Women_, a report into the number of women on the boards of UK grant-making trusts.  
*   In **2016** we launched our New Trust Update archive, an online searchable database of all past issues of the New Trust Update, our monthly summary of newly registered UK grant-makers. The archive grants all subscribers access to all back-issues, and to special reports produced by Factary.  
*   In **2017** we published an in-depth report into the philanthropic activities of the Chairpersons of the UK’s FTSE100. 94 Chairs were profiled, along with their company, including CSR activities.  
*   In **2017** Factary’s Chair and founder, Chris Carnie, published _How Philanthropy is Changing in Europe_ (Policy Press).  
*   In **2017**, in response to regulatory changes and in order to take advantage of new technologies, we designed and pioneered a completely new way to screen and analyse supporter databases to identify major and influential donors, once again proving we are at the forefront of prospect research in the UK.

## General HRI research
### Agricultural robots
[edit]
Human labor has been greatly used in agriculture but Agricultural robots like milking robots have been adopted in large-scale farming. Hygiene is the main issue in the agri-food sector and the invention of this technology has widely impacted agriculture. Robots can also be used in tasks that might be hazardous to human health like in the application of chemicals to plants.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human%E2%80%93robot_interaction#cite_note-80)

Bartneck and Okada[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human%E2%80%93robot_interaction#cite_note-81) suggest that a robotic user interface can be described by the following four properties:
Tool – toy scale
*   Is the system designed to solve a problem effectively or is it just for entertainment?
Remote control – autonomous scale
*   Does the robot require remote control or is it capable of action without direct human influence?
Reactive – dialogue scale
*   Does the robot rely on a fixed interaction pattern or is it able to have dialogue — exchange of information — with a human?
Anthropomorphism scale
*   Does it have the shape or properties of a human?

#### ACE – International Conference on Future Applications of AI, Sensors, and Robotics in Society
[edit]
The International Conference on Future Applications of AI, Sensors, and Robotics in Society explore the state of the art research, highlighting the future challenges as well as the hidden potential behind the technologies. The accepted contributions to this conference will be published annually in the special edition of the Journal of Future Robot Life.

## General HRI research
### Agricultural robots
#### International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots
[edit]
The International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots is an annual congress that invites and encourages a broad range of topics, such as AI, Philosophy, Ethics, Sociology, Engineering, Computer Science, Bioethics.
The earliest academic papers on the subject were presented at the 2006 E.C. Euron Roboethics Atelier, organized by the School of Robotics in Genoa, followed a year later by the first book – "Love and Sex with Robots" – published by Harper Collins in New York. Since that initial flurry of academic activity in this field the subject has grown significantly in breadth and worldwide interest. Three conferences on Human–Robot Personal Relationships were held in the Netherlands during the period 2008–2010, in each case the proceedings were published by respected academic publishers, including Springer-Verlag. After a gap until 2014 the conferences were renamed as the "International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots", which have previously taken place at the University of Madeira in 2014; in London in 2016 and 2017; and in Brussels in 2019. Additionally, the Springer-Verlag "International Journal of Social Robotics", had, by 2016, published articles mentioning the subject, and an open access journal called "Lovotics" was launched in 2012, devoted entirely to the subject. The past few years have also witnessed a strong upsurge of interest by way of increased coverage of the subject in the print media, TV documentaries and feature films, as well as within the academic community.
The International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots provides an opportunity for academics and industry professionals to present and discuss their work and ideas in an academic symposium.

#### IEEE International Symposium in Robot and Human Interactive Communication
[edit]
The IEEE International Symposium on Robot and Human Interactive Communication ( RO-MAN ) was founded in 1992 by Profs. Toshio Fukuda, Hisato Kobayashi, Hiroshi Harashima and Fumio Hara. Early workshop participants were mostly Japanese, and the first seven workshops were held in Japan. Since 1999, workshops have been held in Europe and the United States as well as Japan, and participation has been of international scope.

This conference is one of the most selective in the field of HRI with an average acceptance rate of 26% and an average attendance of 187. Tool – toy scale
*   Is the system designed to solve a problem effectively or is it just for entertainment?
Remote control – autonomous scale
*   Does the robot require remote control or is it capable of action without direct human influence?
Reactive – dialogue scale
*   Does the robot rely on a fixed interaction pattern or is it able to have dialogue — exchange of information — with a human?
Anthropomorphism scale
*   Does it have the shape or properties of a human?

#### International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots
[edit]
The International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots is an annual congress that invites and encourages a broad range of topics, such as AI, Philosophy, Ethics, Sociology, Engineering, Computer Science, Bioethics.
The earliest academic papers on the subject were presented at the 2006 E.C. Euron Roboethics Atelier, organized by the School of Robotics in Genoa, followed a year later by the first book – "Love and Sex with Robots" – published by Harper Collins in New York. Since that initial flurry of academic activity in this field the subject has grown significantly in breadth and worldwide interest. Three conferences on Human–Robot Personal Relationships were held in the Netherlands during the period 2008–2010, in each case the proceedings were published by respected academic publishers, including Springer-Verlag. After a gap until 2014 the conferences were renamed as the "International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots", which have previously taken place at the University of Madeira in 2014; in London in 2016 and 2017; and in Brussels in 2019. Additionally, the Springer-Verlag "International Journal of Social Robotics", had, by 2016, published articles mentioning the subject, and an open access journal called "Lovotics" was launched in 2012, devoted entirely to the subject. The past few years have also witnessed a strong upsurge of interest by way of increased coverage of the subject in the print media, TV documentaries and feature films, as well as within the academic community.
The International Congress on Love and Sex with Robots provides an opportunity for academics and industry professionals to present and discuss their work and ideas in an academic symposium.
